design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS): diagnosis, pathophysiology and treatment. MEDLINE (PubMed and Ovid), Embase, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library, January 2000 to 24 September 2015, English only, plus ClinicalTrials.gov, dissertations, abstracts from four toxicology and emergency-medicine meetings, and reference lists; full search strategies in an appendix. 170 articles included (183 in the abstract): 116 on diagnosis, 61 on pathophysiology (24 of them animal studies) and 13 on treatment, with 80 usable case reports and 8 case series and no randomized trials. Patient-level data from the case reports and 7 of the case series were pooled descriptively into a cumulative synthesis of 211 patients; evidence was rated with GRADE.
can_establish: Which features were commonly described in published cases labelled CHS up to 2015 (recurrent vomiting, abdominal pain, regular and mostly daily use, relief with hot baths or showers, resolution after stopping), and that the evidence on mechanisms and treatment then consisted of case reports, case series, small observational studies and animal work.
cannot_establish: How common CHS is among people who use cannabis (there are no denominators), how well any feature distinguishes CHS from other recurrent vomiting (all patients were selected as CHS cases, usually on those same features, and there is no comparison group, so the reported sensitivities are circular), which frequency, duration, amount or potency of use carries risk, whether any acute treatment works (no controlled study), or the mechanism.

sample.recruitment: Published and grey literature as above (Search Strategy, 1st paragraph; Appendix). The patients are those described in 80 case reports and in case series: Simonetto et al. 2012 (Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 98 patients, entered as the authors' summary statistics because raw data were unavailable), Allen et al. 2004 (9), Soriano-Co et al. 2010 (8), and Sofka & Lerfald 2013, Patterson et al. 2010, Nicolson et al. 2012 and Masri et al. 2012 (4 each). Wallace et al. 2011 (31 patients; by its title a literature review with a proposed diagnosis and treatment algorithm) was left out of the synthesis for lack of raw data (Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Diagnosis: studies of diagnostic criteria, or case reports and series that stated the criteria used. Pathophysiology: animal, human or in vitro models of CHS or cyclic vomiting, or of the endocannabinoid system in vomiting. Treatment: outcomes of behavioural or pharmacological treatments, or animal studies of treatments. Eight case reports were excluded (text inaccessible, not in English, or no final diagnosis of CHS) (Study Selection, 1st paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Cumulative synthesis: 154 men (72.9%) and 57 women (27.1%); median age at diagnosis 28 years (IQR 22 to 34; n = 111), at first cannabis use 16 (14 to 18; n = 84) and at symptom onset 24 (19 to 29; n = 101) (Cumulative Synthesis, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Follow-up was documented for 85 of the 211 patients (40.2%) (Discussion, 10th paragraph); stopping cannabis and its result were documented for 64.
sample.selection_effects: Published cases are a selected sample: the authors acknowledge that clinicians tend to report cases that resemble the index description, and successful treatments (Limitations). Patients entered because their clinicians diagnosed CHS, usually using the very features whose frequencies are then reported. One series (Simonetto et al. 2012) supplies 98 of the 211 patients, as summary statistics. English-only search; the countries of the cases are not tabulated.

exposure.measurement: As described in each report, in heterogeneous units (cones, bongs, joints, cigarettes, grams per day); the reviewers coded heavy use as daily and frequent use as weekly (Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Limitations). No biological verification of use is synthesized.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency (211 patients): more than daily 50 (23.7%), daily 101 (47.9%), weekly 41 (19.4%), less than weekly 5 (2.4%), not specified 14 (6.6%). Duration of use before symptom onset (179 patients): 1 year or less 45 (25.1%), 2 to 5 years 65 (36.3%), 6 to 10 years 30 (16.8%), 11 years or more 39 (21.8%) (Cumulative Synthesis, 1st paragraph). Route, product and potency were not synthesized; three cases involved synthetic cannabinoids (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Stopping cannabis was documented for 64 patients; whether abstinence was verified is not systematically reported (the two patients whose symptoms did not resolve had no urine testing) (Treatment of CHS, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: None in the case synthesis. Comparisons appear only in second-hand studies of cyclic vomiting syndrome (Table 4), for example a case-control study published in a journal supplement (Fajardo et al. 2005) and a Colorado before-and-after study (Kim et al. 2015).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Cyclic vomiting syndrome, migraine, gastroparesis, psychiatric conditions and other drug use before cannabis use were not extracted; the authors discuss the diagnostic overlap with cyclic vomiting syndrome (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Features as recorded in case reports and series; 14 diagnostic characteristics drawn from 7 published diagnostic frameworks (Allen 2004; Sontineni 2009; Simonetto 2012; Pattathan 2012; Sun 2013; Cheung 2014; Morris 2014) (Tables 2 and 7). Treatment outcomes as reported, mainly resolution of symptoms.
outcomes.validity_norms: No reference standard: the frequencies are of features among diagnosed cases. GRADE was applied to individual studies as well as to outcomes (Assessment of Study Quality, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: Frequency of each characteristic = patients with it divided by patients for whom it was reported (Data Analysis, 2nd paragraph); denominators range from 64 to 227. Four characteristics were too inconsistently documented to count (return of symptoms on resuming use, normal bowel habits, negative medical workup, weight loss over 5 kg).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers screened all titles independently and settled disagreements by consensus; who abstracted the data, and whether in duplicate, is not stated (Study Selection; Data Collection).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive frequencies only (Table 2): cyclic vomiting 100% (211), severe nausea and vomiting 100% (211), abdominal pain 85.1% (202), relief with hot bathing 92.3% (157 of 170), resolution after stopping cannabis 96.8% (62 of 64), at least weekly use 97.4% (197), daily use 76.6% (197), regular use for more than a year 74.8% (179), male 72.9% (denominator printed as 227), age under 50 100% (227 as printed). Of the cases with raw data, 85 met at least four and 104 at least three of the six characteristics proposed in the Discussion (75.2% and 92%; the denominator is printed as 133, while these percentages imply 113, the number of cases with raw data in Table 1; editors' calculation). Mean delay from symptom onset to diagnosis 4.1 years (SD 4.6; n not stated). Second-hand association estimates from studies of cyclic vomiting are in Table 4 (key findings).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the review says it followed PRISMA.
analysis.selective_reporting: Treatment numbers for the same case series differ between the text and Table 5, the evidence grade for stopping cannabis differs between Table 5, the Results and the Discussion, and the abstract and Results give different numbers of included articles (see reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 211 published cases labelled CHS, all had recurrent vomiting, most had abdominal pain, most used cannabis daily or more, about a quarter had used for a year or less before symptoms began, and nearly all of those whose bathing or stopping was documented reported relief with hot water (157 of 170) or resolution after stopping (62 of 64; stopping was documented for only 64). There were no controlled studies of diagnosis or treatment; acute treatments rest on single case reports and a 5-patient series published as a one-page report; every proposed mechanism was rated very low.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Results say the listed features have "the highest sensitivity for identifying patients with CHS" (Cumulative Synthesis, 4th paragraph). Gaps: (1) sensitivity cannot be estimated from cases selected by those same features, and specificity was not studied; (2) the Discussion (4th paragraph) speaks of moderate evidence that stopping cannabis is the definitive treatment, while the Results grade it low and Table 5 very low, and the review's own GRADE definitions place case series at very low; (3) the Discussion (5th paragraph) calls its output evidence-based recommendations and guidelines for treatment, and later calls for public-health warnings, on case-level evidence; (4) the introduction lists CHS among the more common adverse effects of cannabis, while the review contains no frequency data and itself calls for studies of prevalence; (5) the abstract reports regular use for any duration in 100% of patients, while the Results give regular use for more than a year in 74.8%; (6) the introduction describes CHS as a syndrome of chronic, high-dose use, while 25% had used for a year or less and 19% weekly. The Limitations section, on the other hand, states the publication bias and incomplete reporting plainly.

timeline.event: Allen et al. (Gut): first description of cannabinoid hyperemesis, a case series (9 patients in this review's Table 1) and the first of the seven diagnostic frameworks.
Sontineni et al.: proposed diagnostic criteria (one of the seven frameworks).
Wallace et al.: literature review with a proposed diagnosis and treatment algorithm (31 patients), cited as treatment evidence but left out of the cumulative synthesis.

Simonetto et al. (Mayo Clin Proc): case series of 98 patients, the largest source of the cumulative synthesis, and a diagnostic framework; Pattathan et al. framework from a study of marijuana use and cyclic vomiting syndrome.
Sun & Zimmermann framework; Hickey et al. case report of haloperidol treatment.
Cheung et al. and Morris & Fisher frameworks; LaPoint case series of five patients treated with capsaicin cream (a one-page report in Clinical Toxicology).
Kim et al. (Acad Emerg Med): cyclic vomiting presentations nearly doubled after cannabis liberalization in Colorado (prevalence ratio 1.92); co-authored by this review's senior author.
This review (online December 2016): by its authors' account the first and most comprehensive characterization of the CHS literature.

replication.where_it_stands: The case-based picture assembled here (recurrent vomiting with regular, mostly daily use, relief with hot water, resolution after stopping) underlies later clinical descriptions, but no study in this review measured how common CHS is or tested a treatment against a control. Later treatment studies are covered by the project's card for Sabbineni et al. (2024) (sc_sabbineni_2024); nothing later was read for this card. The case series inside the synthesis (Allen 2004, Simonetto 2012 and others) must not be cited as independent support alongside this review.

funding.funder: No funding statement for the review itself. Author support as printed: Borgelt, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment and the University of Colorado Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences; Phillips, NIH (printed as NIH on Drug Abuse) R15 DA041656 and R01 DA034957; Monte, NIH 1 K23 GM110516 and NIH CTSI UL1 TR001082. The Acknowledgements thank the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee.
funding.declared_conflicts: Sorensen and DeSanto declare no conflicts of interest; for the other three authors only the support listed above is given (Compliance with Ethical Standards › Funding and Financial Disclosures).
funding.affiliations_note: Denver Health, the University of Colorado (emergency medicine, the health sciences library, pharmacy), the University of Northern Colorado and the Rocky Mountain Poison & Drug Center. The senior author (Monte) is an author of Kim et al. (2015), the Colorado study cited for the near doubling of cyclic-vomiting presentations (Table 4). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people who use cannabis, with frequency, duration, product and potency measured and recurrent vomiting ascertained with standard criteria, to estimate incidence by pattern of use; a diagnostic-accuracy study in consecutive patients with recurrent vomiting, with and without cannabis use, comparing the proposed CHS criteria against resolution after verified, sustained abstinence; and randomized trials of acute treatments against an active comparator or placebo.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Three broad questions (diagnosis, pathophysiology, treatment) with eligibility by topic; no comparator, no defined treatment outcomes and no reference standard for diagnosis.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Every design (case reports, case series, observational, animal and in vitro studies) was admitted without an explanation; the absence of trials is reported only as a result.

Four databases with full strategies in the appendix, grey literature (trial registry, dissertations, four conferences) and reference lists; but English only and from January 2000, neither justified (the language limit is named only as a limitation), which is no under decision p-amstar2-item4. The date limit also excludes earlier mechanistic and animal work on cannabinoids and vomiting.
Two reviewers independently reviewed all titles, obtained the full texts of relevant articles and settled disagreements by consensus (Study Selection).
Who abstracted the data, and whether in duplicate, is not stated (Data Collection).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded full-text articles and no flow diagram; only the excluded case reports are cited, with grouped reasons (8 said to be excluded, 11 references given).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The case series are described in Table 1 (size, sex, ages, duration and frequency of use, features); individual case reports are not tabulated, and the pathophysiology and treatment studies are summarised with their design in Tables 3 to 5.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias tool was applied to the included studies; GRADE levels were assigned to studies largely by design, which does not assess selection, measurement or reporting bias in case reports.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: No meta-analysis (the authors say study quality precluded it). The descriptive cumulative synthesis mixes patient-level case data with one series' summary statistics, and its denominators vary by characteristic.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Without an appraisal of the included studies the interpretation could not account for their risk of bias; the Limitations discuss publication and reporting bias in the literature, but the Discussion then grades stopping cannabis as moderate evidence and presents the characteristics as the most sensitive.
Heterogeneity is mentioned only as incomplete and inconsistent reporting; differences between sources (for example the 98-patient series against the individual case reports) are not examined.
No meta-analysis; publication bias is acknowledged qualitatively in the Limitations.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Author support and the absence of conflicts for two authors are declared; no funding is stated for the review itself, and the senior author's authorship of a cited study (Kim et al. 2015) is not mentioned.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Critical items 2, 4, 7, 9 and 13 are not met (11 and 15 do not apply), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. This rates how far the review's summaries can be trusted as unbiased syntheses, not whether its descriptions are wrong: the review collects the case literature transparently, publishes its search strategies and states the publication bias plainly. Practical consequences: the feature frequencies describe published cases selected by those features and should not be called sensitivities; the treatment evidence is anecdotal; and the review's GRADE ratings are internally inconsistent and should not be quoted as an independent grading. It may be cited for the case-based description of CHS (with its denominators), for the absence of controlled evidence up to 2015, and as a pointer to the primary reports.

key_findings.finding: The search returned 2,154 records plus 24 from bibliographies; 1,253 abstracts were screened and 170 articles included: 116 on diagnosis, 61 on pathophysiology (including 24 animal studies) and 13 on treatment, with 88 case reports (8 excluded) and 8 case series of four or more patients; no randomized trials of diagnosis, pathophysiology or treatment were found, and the low quality of the articles precluded meta-analysis.
key_findings.note: The abstract gives 183 included articles (see reporting issues). The database counts in the appendix (34 + 1,099 + 341 + 357 + 323) sum to 2,154 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Cumulative synthesis of 211 patients (80 case reports and 7 case series): 154 men (72.9%) and 57 women; median age at diagnosis 28 years (IQR 22 to 34; n = 111), at first cannabis use 16 (14 to 18; n = 84) and at symptom onset 24 (19 to 29; n = 101); cannabis use is said to have preceded symptom onset in all cases.
key_findings.note: The three median ages rest only on the 113 patients with individual data: each n equals the sum of the Table 1 rows without the 98-patient Simonetto series, which gave only means (32.3 years at diagnosis, 25.3 at symptom onset; editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Pattern of use before symptoms: frequency reported for 211 patients, more than daily 50 (23.7%), daily 101 (47.9%), weekly 41 (19.4%), less than weekly 5 (2.4%), not specified 14 (6.6%); duration of use before symptom onset reported for 179, 1 year or less 45 (25.1%), 2 to 5 years 65 (36.3%), 6 to 10 years 30 (16.8%), 11 years or more 39 (21.8%).
key_findings.locator: Cumulative Synthesis, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Cumulative synthesis row)
key_findings.note: Quantities were reported in heterogeneous units; heavy use was coded as daily and frequent use as weekly (Data Analysis, 1st paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Frequency of the major characteristics among cases where each was reported: cyclic vomiting 100% (211), severe nausea and vomiting 100% (211), abdominal pain 85.1% (202), relief with hot baths or showers 92.3% (157 of 170), resolution after stopping cannabis 96.8% (62 of 64), at least weekly use 97.4% (197), daily use 76.6% (197), regular use for more than 1 year 74.8% (179), male 72.9% and age under 50 100% (denominators printed as 227); all graded low. Return of symptoms on resuming use, normal bowel habits, negative workup and weight loss over 5 kg were too inconsistently documented to count.
key_findings.note: These are proportions of published, clinician-diagnosed cases, not sensitivities; the resolution figure rests on 64 patients whose stopping was documented.

key_findings.finding: Stopping cannabis: among 64 patients with documented cessation, 62 (96.8%) had complete resolution of symptoms; the two without resolution had no urine testing to confirm abstinence; all 21 patients who did not abstain had ongoing symptoms. Case series cited in the text: Wallace et al. 24 of 25, Allen et al. 7 of 7, Simonetto et al. 6 of 6, Patterson et al. 4 of 4, Soriano-Co et al. 4 of 5.
key_findings.note: Table 5 gives different numbers for some of the same series (see reporting issues); the evidence for stopping is graded very low (Table 5), low (Results) and moderate (Discussion). The text attributes the two patients without resolution to two case reports (refs 8 and 56: Cox et al. 2012; Parikh & Gould 2010, a meeting abstract), while Table 1 places one in the Soriano-Co series (4 of 5) and one among the case reports (37 of 38); Table 1 heads the column relief with abstinence or reduction, while the text speaks of documented cessation. With the Simonetto discrepancy (reporting issue 5), the details behind 62 of 64 cannot be reproduced from the review's own tables.

key_findings.finding: Acute treatments: evidence for dopamine antagonists consists of a single case report of haloperidol (Hickey et al. 2013) and a one-page report in Clinical Toxicology (Witsil et al. 2013); for capsaicin cream on the abdomen, a case series of 5 patients with complete or near-complete resolution (LaPoint 2014) and a case report (Biary et al. 2014), both one-page reports in Clinical Toxicology; avoiding opioids rests on a consensus statement on opioid-induced constipation (Argoff et al. 2015) and a review (Galli et al. 2011), with no direct evidence; all graded very low. Dehydration and acute renal failure requiring fluids are described in case reports.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of CHS, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 5

key_findings.finding: Mechanisms: nine proposed mechanisms (for example CB1-mediated emetic and anti-emetic effects, reduced gut motility, CB1 down-regulation with rebound, accumulation of cannabinoids in fat, a non-THC plant compound, genetic variation in metabolising enzymes, splanchnic vasodilation relieved by hot bathing) are all graded very low; the authors call CB1 agonism the most parsimonious explanation, supported by animal and in vitro studies, and note three cases caused by synthetic cannabinoids.
key_findings.locator: Pathophysiology of CHS, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Second-hand studies of cyclic vomiting syndrome (CVS): after cannabis liberalization in Colorado, CVS presentations nearly doubled (prevalence ratio 1.92, 95% CI 1.33 to 2.79) and patients were more likely to have cannabis use documented (OR 3.59, 1.44 to 9.00) (Kim et al. 2015); among 437 CVS patients, 81% used cannabis and 67% used hot showers for relief, and bathing was associated with cannabis use (OR 2.54, 1.2 to 4.3) (Venkatesan et al. 2013, journal supplement); 22% of CVS cases against 12% of controls used cannabis (OR 2.1, 0.7 to 6.1) (Fajardo et al. 2005, journal supplement); in smaller CVS series 72% of 31 used hot showers and 42% used cannabis daily to weekly (Namin et al. 2007), and 12 of 20 used cannabis chronically (Oruganti et al. 2010, journal supplement).
key_findings.note: Second-hand; Venkatesan, Fajardo and Oruganti are cited to journal supplements (supplement page numbers), so their methods cannot be checked from full papers; the Venkatesan interval and P value are inconsistent as reported here (see reporting issues). Kim et al. is an ecological before-and-after comparison co-authored by this review's senior author.

key_findings.finding: Of the cases with raw data, 85 met at least four and 104 at least three of the six characteristics proposed in the Discussion (75.2% and 92%).
key_findings.note: The denominator is printed as 133; the percentages correspond to 113, the number of cases with raw data in Table 1 (80 + 9 + 8 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4; editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Delay and health-care use: mean delay from symptom onset to diagnosis 4.1 years (SD 4.6; n not stated); an early series of 8 cases averaged 7.1 emergency department visits, 3.1 hospitalizations and 5.0 clinic visits before diagnosis (Soriano-Co et al. 2010); a multicentre cohort published in a journal supplement found means of 5.3 abdominal CT scans, 3.8 ultrasounds and 5.5 abdominal radiographs, and a median charge of $95,023 for 7 patients at one emergency department (Perrotta et al. 2012).
key_findings.locator: Cumulative Synthesis, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 8th paragraph; Introduction, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The charge interval $62,420 to $268,110 is called an IQR in the introduction and a range in the Discussion.

key_findings.finding: Diagnostic overlaps: four case reports of patients first diagnosed with hyperemesis gravidarum and later with CHS; in the Simonetto et al. series, 18 of 61 patients (30%) who had gastric emptying studies showed delayed emptying, which the authors say should not preclude a CHS diagnosis.
Follow-up was documented for only 85 of 211 patients (40.2%).

The authors' proposed diagnostic characteristics, each graded low: severe cyclic vomiting usually with abdominal pain; symptom onset preceded by at least weekly cannabis use; temporary relief with hot bathing; resolution with stopping cannabis; supportive features male sex, cannabis use starting in the teenage years and symptom onset in the third decade of life.

Return of symptoms on resuming use is counted as too inconsistently documented to give a frequency (Table 2), but Table 5 relays that in Allen et al.'s series all 3 patients who used cannabis again after a period of abstinence had a return of illness (Table 5 gives that series 10 patients, Table 1 gives 9).
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis of CHS, 1st paragraph; Table 2; Table 5 (Cessation of cannabis, Allen row)
key_findings.note: A single small series; the review does not count it in Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 183 articles were included; the Results say 170.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the evidence base cannot be stated exactly; use 170 with the breakdown given in the Results.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives a history of regular cannabis use for any duration in 100% of patients; the Results and Table 2 give regular use for more than a year in 74.8% (179 patients) and do not report a 100% figure for regular use of any duration.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Diagnosis of CHS, 1st paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim about duration of use should use the Results figure (a quarter had used for a year or less).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives the denominator for male sex and for age under 50 as 227, but the cumulative synthesis has 211 patients; 154 men are 73.0% of 211 and 67.8% of 227, so the printed 72.9% matches 211 (editors' calculation). The text also says age under 50 at evaluation, Table 2 at onset of illness.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2; Cumulative Synthesis, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; quote 154 of 211. Several other printed shares are truncated rather than rounded (157 of 170 is 92.4%, printed 92.3; 62 of 64 is 96.9%, printed 96.8; 192 of 197 is 97.5%, printed 97.4; 134 of 179 is 74.9%, printed 74.8; 85 of 211 is 40.3%, printed 40.2; editors' calculation); claims may quote the printed values.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that 85 (75.2%) of 133 cases with raw data met at least four characteristics and 104 (92%) at least three; 85 and 104 of 133 are 63.9% and 78.2%, whereas of 113 (the cases with raw data in Table 1) they are 75.2% and 92.0% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator is very probably 113; with 133 the percentages would be much lower.

reporting_issues.issue: Results for the same case series differ between the text and Table 5: Wallace et al., 24 of 25 resolved after stopping (text and Table 1) against 30 of 31 (Table 5); Simonetto et al., 6 of 6 (text and Table 1) against a Table 5 description of 10 followed up, of whom 60% stopped and resolved, 30% continued with symptoms and one had no improvement despite reported abstinence; Allen et al., 9 patients (Table 1) against 10 (Table 5).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Treatment of CHS, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 5
reporting_issues.consequence: The resolution figures of individual series are unreliable as printed; the pooled 62 of 64 comes from Table 1, which excludes Wallace et al.

reporting_issues.issue: The evidence for stopping cannabis is graded very low in Table 5, low in the Results and moderate in the Discussion; the diagnostic characteristics, drawn from case reports and series, are graded low in Tables 2 and 6 although the review's own definitions place case series and case reports at very low.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Assessment of Study Quality, 1st paragraph; Treatment of CHS, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Tables 2, 5 and 6
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's GRADE ratings cannot be quoted as a consistent grading; the encyclopedia should grade the underlying evidence itself.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference numbers are wrong in several places: Table 1 cites Simonetto et al. as [12] (Soriano-Co's number) and Patterson et al. as [10] (Wallace's number); Table 5 cites Simonetto as [16], which is a letter; PRISMA and GRADE are both cited to [83], the GRADE paper; the text cites five observational CVS studies as [175 to 179], but [176] is a review and the fifth study in Table 4 is [187].
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Tables 1, 4 and 5; Search Strategy; References 9 to 16, 83, 175 to 179 and 187
reporting_issues.consequence: Sources must be identified by author and year, not by the printed numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: Some citations do not support the statements they are attached to: the genetic-variation hypothesis and plant variability are cited to [131], an analytical method for THC and metabolites in blood; the CB1 mechanism in Table 3 is cited partly to [135], a study of cannabis dependence and withdrawal in adolescents; Table 5 labels Galli et al. 2011, a review, as a case report.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Pathophysiology of CHS, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tables 3 and 5; References 131, 135 and 170
reporting_issues.consequence: The mechanism table should not be used as a map of evidence; its very-low ratings are, if anything, generous for some rows.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the Sofka & Lerfald series (4 patients) has a median age at symptom onset of 14 (IQR 11.5 to 16.5), below its median age at first cannabis use of 16 (14.5 to 17.5); if every patient's symptoms began after first use, as the text says of all cases, the median onset could not be lower than the median first use (editors' reasoning). Soriano-Co et al. has a median onset of 30.5 outside its own IQR (32.4 to 32.4), and the Sofka sample size is printed as n = −4.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1; Cumulative Synthesis, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Errors in the extracted case data; the statement that use preceded symptoms in all cases cannot be checked for these series.

reporting_issues.issue: As reported in Table 4 and the Discussion, the Venkatesan et al. association of bathing with cannabis use (OR 2.54, 95% CI 1.2 to 4.3, P = 0.0006) is internally inconsistent: the interval implies a two-sided P of about 0.004 to 0.01, and its log-scale midpoint is an OR of 2.27 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Second-hand from an item in a journal supplement; check the primary before quoting the estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: Wallace et al. (2011), whose title describes a literature review with a proposed algorithm, is tabulated as a case series of 31 patients and used as treatment evidence, while being left out of the cumulative synthesis for lack of raw data; whether its patients overlap with the case reports pooled in the synthesis is not discussed.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 (footnote b); Table 5; Reference 10
reporting_issues.consequence: Possible double counting in the treatment evidence; Wallace et al. should not be cited as an independent series.

reporting_issues.issue: Eight case reports are said to have been excluded, but eleven references (108 to 118) are given for them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the excluded set cannot be reconstructed exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: Time to improvement of symptoms with abstinence is listed among the data extracted from each report, but no result for it is given anywhere in the review.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Materials and Methods › Data Collection, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: No time course of recovery after stopping can be cited from this review.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC5330965 (Journal of Medical Toxicology version of record): all sections, Tables 1 to 7 rendered as text with their footnotes, the appendix of search strategies, Compliance with Ethical Standards (funding and financial disclosures), Acknowledgements, author affiliations and the full reference list; Figure 1 (frequency of use) is an image whose values are given in the text; there is no flow diagram and no supplementary material. No correction is linked from the page.

disagreements.reviewer: Second reader 218, key finding 1 note and missed item 3: the median ages come only from the 113 cases with raw data.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted. Table 1 in the saved text: diagnosis 9+8+4+4+4+4+78 = 111, first use 9+8+4+4+4+2+53 = 84, onset 9+8+4+4+4+4+68 = 101; Simonetto reports means only and Wallace is outside the synthesis.

disagreements.first_pass: the evidence for stopping is graded very low (Table 5), low (Results) and moderate (Discussion).
disagreements.reviewer: Second reader 218, missed items 1 and 2: attribution of the two non-resolvers differs between text and Table 1; Table 1's column counts abstinence or reduction.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted. Treatment of CHS, 1st paragraph (refs 8 and 56), Table 1 rows and column heading, and references 8 and 56 checked in the saved text.

disagreements.reviewer: Second reader 218, missed item 5: Table 5 relays that all 3 of Allen et al.'s patients who resumed relapsed.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted and added as a key finding after checking Tables 2 and 5 in the saved text.
